rows.evidence: Q1: Section 4.1 Experimental analysis and Figures 7-8 - the authors built a prototype (Node.js server, five virtual blockchain nodes, Arduino/NodeMCU sensor nodes for soil humidity, temperature and water level) and report real-time sensor traces from two fields and the average response time of the system.
rows.notes: The study is a design-and-prototype paper. Its only reported results are sensor monitoring traces (soil humidity, temperature, soil-irrigation level, water storage litres used/left) and the average response time of the EBMA-IoT framework (Figure 8). It does not measure trust, coordination, water sharing or any social outcome among farmers; the claim that blockchain builds trust among community members competing for scarce resources is asserted in the introduction and conclusion, not tested. The sensed variables are soil humidity, temperature and water level rather than flow metering as such, though Figure 7d shows litres of water used. The data availability statement says no new data were created or analysed, which reinforces that the paper offers no evidence on the claimed effect. At most it demonstrates a precondition (secure monitoring and storage of water data).

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 4.1 Experimental analysis and Figures 7-8 - prototype implementation with Arduino-based soil humidity, temperature and water level sensors, five virtual blockchain nodes and reported average response time.
rows.notes: No result on water-use efficiency or water saving is reported. The study only shows that the prototype senses soil humidity/temperature, indicates when soil reaches 100% irrigation level, displays water used/left (Figure 7d), and reports the average response time for executing irrigation rules (Figure 8). No comparison of water applied with or without the system, no crop or yield data, no water productivity metric. Claims about efficient water use are assertions in the introduction and conclusion. The paper demonstrates monitoring capability, a precondition of the claimed conservation effect, not the effect itself. Sensors are soil/water-level rather than flow meters, noted but not treated as a full technology mismatch since water volume used is displayed.

notes: Full text appears complete (13 pages). The paper is largely conceptual (architecture, design patterns, authentication protocol) with a thin prototype evaluation limited to response time and raw sensor traces; the data availability statement explicitly says no new data were created or analysed. Q1 was answered yes on the basis of the reported prototype experiment, but the study provides no evidence of its own on either claimed effect.
